title: The powers by birth, herbs, mantra, discipline, samadhi (4.1)
hook: the last book opens by listing five places powers can come from, and only one of them is samadhi

segments.voice: Yesterday: kaivalya, and your line, equal. When the mind is as clear as the seer, freedom, with or without the powers. Did you wipe the glass once? Day four hundred eighty.

A hummingbird hangs in the air outside a kitchen window, perfectly still, wings a blur. No human being has ever done that on their own. Yet the hummingbird never meditated a day in its life. It didn't fast, didn't chant, didn't study. It was born that way. Hovering is just what its body does. Hold onto that bird. Book four of the Yoga Sutras, the last and shortest book, is called Kaivalya, freedom. And its very first sutra is about where powers come from. The hummingbird is the first answer.
screen: `A HUMMINGBIRD HOVERS.` → `IT NEVER MEDITATED.` → `BORN THAT WAY.`

segments.voice: Sutra 4.1: the powers are born of birth, herbs, mantra, discipline or samadhi. Five sources. Birth: some abilities come with the body you're born into. The classical commentary speaks of powers that come with birth into another kind of body. A bird is born to fly. Herbs: the commentary mentions elixirs, potions said to be found in the realms of the asuras. Mantra: sacred sound, recited with power. Discipline, tapas: the heat of austerity. And samadhi: everything book three has been describing. Now ask why the book of freedom opens here. One answer: it puts the powers in their place. If an ability can come from birth, or from an herb, then an ability on its own proves nothing about someone's inner life. A hummingbird hovers, and nobody calls it enlightened. Patanjali has already told us the powers are obstacles in samadhi. Here he adds: they're not even unique to yoga. Five doors lead to them. Only one of those doors is samadhi. And over the next few sutras, he'll say that the mind born of meditation is the one that leaves no new karma behind. So the list isn't a menu. It's a quiet sorting. Book four is short, thirty-four sutras, and it's headed somewhere bigger than any power: the nature of mind, karma, time, and finally freedom itself. But first it clears the table. Five sources, and none of them is the point.
screen: `BIRTH, HERBS, MANTRA.` · `DISCIPLINE, AND SAMADHI.` · `A POWER ALONE PROVES NOTHING.` · `ONLY ONE DOOR IS SAMADHI.` · then, large: `FIVE SOURCES.`

segments.voice: Today's practice notices what you were simply given. Sit steady and easy, and rest on the breath. The breath itself is a gift of birth. You didn't earn it. Feel it come, without your effort. Then think of one ability you have that you never really worked for: a good ear, a quick laugh, patience with children. Hold it lightly, without pride, without dismissing it. Just: this came with me. Then come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
The powers by birth. The first of five sources in sutra 4.1: birth, herbs, mantra, discipline and samadhi.
Your line: five sources. Today, when someone impresses you, or you impress yourself, ask where that ability came from before deciding what it says about anyone. Day four hundred eighty.

screen: `DAY 480 COUNTS.` → `BOOK FOUR BEGINS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MIND'S TRANSFORMATIONS FROM NATURE.`

howItsDone: Hindu traditions recognize many sources of extraordinary ability, including birth, medicinal preparations, mantra and austerity, and teachers of the Yoga Sutras use 4.1 to remind students that such abilities are not in themselves signs of liberation.

fork.reveal: 4.1 lists five sources of powers. only one is samadhi, so an ability on its own proves nothing about someone's inner life.

original.note: Sanskrit oṣadhi: herb, medicinal plant; the second of the five sources of powers in 4.1.

trapdoor: what you thought: powers are the reward for deep spiritual practice.
what it means: powers can come from birth, herbs, mantra, discipline or samadhi, so they prove nothing on their own.
what a scholar hears: janmaushadhi-mantra-tapah-samadhija siddhayah (4.1), opening the Kaivalya Pada; the Bhashya's rasayana in the abodes of the asuras.

notes: Bhashya on 4.1: powers from birth (deha-antara, in another body) and herbs (rasayana in the abodes of the asuras): confirm.
The hummingbird is the script's illustration of 'birth', not from the commentary.
The reading of 4.1 as 'putting the powers in their place' is a common teaching reading; a Keeper may wish to name it as such.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the bird-born-to-fly gloss is no longer attributed to the Bhashya; the closing instruction to the listener became a statement. 'The last and shortest book' and 'thirty-four sutras' kept as counts from the cited text; confirm.
